title: Year two opens: back in the cycle
hook: last year stopped at Va'era; this year the Torah is read through to its last word

segments.voice: Yesterday we stood at the big lookout and said Shehecheyanu, blessing the arriving. Your line was you kept me alive for this. Now the path turns into year two.

A Torah scroll is two wooden rollers with a long ribbon of parchment wound between them. On Shabbat morning someone opens it on the reading table, and it's already sitting where last week's reading stopped. Nobody rewinds to the start because they missed a week. Nobody skips ahead to the good part. The scroll simply waits where it was left. Last year's reading stopped in the middle of Exodus, in a portion called Va'era, with hail and fire falling on Egypt together. Year two picks up from exactly there.
screen: `TWO ROLLERS, ONE LONG RIBBON.` → `IT WAITS WHERE YOU LEFT IT.` → `LAST YEAR STOPPED AT VA'ERA.`

segments.voice: The Torah, the five books of Moses, is divided into weekly portions. Each one is called a parashah, which simply means a section; plenty of people say parsha. Each is named for an early, distinctive word in it. Bereshit, in the beginning. Va'era, and I appeared. Next comes Bo, which means come. Across the Jewish year the portions are read in order, and in weeks when the calendar runs short, two are read together so the whole thing fits. That's a one-year cycle. The Talmud remembers that Jews in the Land of Israel once took three years to finish, and today some congregations read a third of each portion, on a three-year rhythm of their own. Either way, the end is not an end. On the holiday of Simchat Torah, the last lines of Deuteronomy are read, and straight after them, the first lines of Genesis. People dance with the scrolls in their arms. The circle closes and opens in the same morning. The sayings of the fathers keep a line from a sage called Ben Bag Bag about the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it. A year-two reader turns it again. The plan: the rest of Exodus, Bo to the finished tabernacle. Then Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, to the very last word. Then the siddur, the prayer book, page by page. Then the Jewish year, in depth.
screen: `WEEKLY PORTIONS: PARASHAH.` · `NAMED FOR AN EARLY WORD.` · `ONE YEAR, OR THREE.` · `SIMCHAT TORAH: THE END MEETS THE START.` · then, large: `TURN IT AND TURN IT.`

segments.voice: Picture the scroll lying open at the spot where you left it, waiting, not annoyed that you were gone. Now think of one thing in your own life you set down and meant to pick up again, a book, a habit, a conversation, and without scolding yourself, just notice where your marker is.
Parashah. A section — the name for each weekly Torah portion, picked up this year right where last year's reading left off, at Bo.
Your line: the scroll keeps rolling. It waits right where you left it, no starting over. Year two, day one.

howItsDone: Synagogues read one Torah portion each Shabbat, in order, across the year; on Simchat Torah the last lines of Deuteronomy are read and the first lines of Genesis follow at once. Some Jews also study the week's portion at home.

chat.meaning: The portions are read in order, and the scroll opens where last week's reading stopped. Nobody rewinds or skips ahead.

parashah.meaning: a section; the name for each weekly Torah portion

Va'era.meaning: and I appeared; the portion where year one stopped

Simchat Torah.meaning: the holiday when the Torah's last and first lines are read

Ben Bag Bag.meaning: an early sage: turn it and turn it, everything is in it

sources.ref: Simchat Torah reading: Deuteronomy 33–34 and Genesis 1

notes: Fifty-four portions is the standard count; in many years some are combined. Confirm phrasing.

Triennial cycle: Megillah 29b mentions 'the people of the West' (Land of Israel) completing the Torah in three years. The modern triennial reading in some Conservative and Reform congregations is a different arrangement; described loosely as a three-year rhythm with ancient roots. Check.
Ben Bag Bag's saying is Avot 5:22 in common numbering (5:25/5:26 in some); paraphrased.
'Longer than a city bus' for a fully unrolled scroll: Torah scrolls vary, commonly tens of meters; verify the image is safe.
The path's order (rest of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, then siddur, then the Jewish year) follows the y2.md header; the teach states it as the plan.
